8. Before proceeding further let us go through the relevant provisions of law.
The main ingredients of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are as follows:
( a) The accused issued a cheque on an account maintained by him with a bank.
(b) The said cheque has been issued in discharge of any legal debt or other liability.

(c) The cheque has been presented to the bank within the period of six months from the date of the cheque or within the period of CA No. 77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 7 OF 25 its validity.

sentences.text: (d) When the aforesaid cheque was presented for encashment, the same was returned unpaid/dishonoured.
(e) The Payee of the cheque issued a legal notice of demand within 30 days from the receipt of information by him from the Bank regarding the return of the cheque.
(f) The Drawer of the cheque failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the aforesaid legal notice of demand.
If the aforesaid ingredients are satisfied then the drawer of the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence punishable u/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act.
8.1 Under Section 139 of the NI Act, unless the contrary is proved, the holder of a cheque shall be presumed to have received the cheque in discharge of any debt or other liability.
Sub clause (a) of Section 118 of the NI Act, inter-alia provides that unless the contrary is proved, a drawn up negotiable instrument, if accepted, has to be presumed to be for consideration.

In Goa Plast (P) Ltd.
vs. Chico Ursula D'souza & Anr., (2003) 3 SCC 232, Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that the provisions of Section 138 to 142 of the NI Act, is for the purpose of giving credibility to negotiable instruments in business transactions.

8.6 At this juncture, reference to section 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act is essential.

"91. Evidence of contracts, grants and other dispositions of property reduced to form of document When the terms of contract, or of a grant, or of any other disposition of property, have been reduced to the form of a document, and in all cases in which any matter is required by law to be reduced to the form of a document, no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such contract, grant or other disposition of property,
or of such matter, except the document itself, or secondary evidence of its contents in cases in which secondary evidence is admissible under the provisions hereinabove contained.
Exception ..................................."
"92. Exclusion of evidence of oral agreement When the terms of any such contract,
grantor other disposition of property, or any matter required by law to be reduced to the form of document have been proved according to the last CA No. 77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 11 OF 25 section, no evidence of any oral agreement of statement shall be admitted, as between the parties to any such instrument of their representatives in interest, for purpose of contradicting, varying, adding to, or subtracting from, it terms; Provision(1) - Any fact may be proved which would invalidate any document, or which would entitle any person to any decree or order relating thereto; such as fraud, intimidation, illegality,
want of due execution, want of capacity in any contracting party, (want or failure) of consideration, or mistake in fact or law Proviso (2)..........
Proviso (3).........."
9. Section 91, inter alia, stipulates that where the terms of contract or of a grant or any other disposition of property have been reduced to a form of written document - no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such a contract, grant or other disposition of property, except the document itself.

Therefore, if there is a written contract executed, neither party can claim that the terms of the contract or the nature of transaction/disposition is, in fact, different from that contained in the document itself.

As per the said term, the second party has received sum of Rs.50,00,000/- in whole, partly in cash and partly through cheques on the date of execution of the agreement.
In view of the same, judgment so cited can very well be distinguished on facts from the facts in hand.

10.8 Coming to the second judgment i.e. Gurdip Singh Anand Vs. Joseph Daniel (supra) the amount of loan so advanced was inclusive of the interest which is not the situation in the present case since there is a separate clause of interest as clause (4) in the loan agreement which is "that second party is bound to pay Rs.6,00,000/- after every 45 days if they fail to pay the interest then whole will become due as interest on amount, which five cheques become due.".

entities.text: Gurdip Singh Anand Vs. Joseph Daniel
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The third judgment so relied from the side of the appellant is also quite distinguishable in facts from the facts in hand.

10.9 Secondly, the appellant has contended that the impugned judgment is bad in law and fact since it fails to take into account order dated 22.11.2017 passed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Cr. Misc. Case No. 3018 of 2017 between the same parties wherein the Hon'ble High Court is pleased to observe that it is also noted that litigation regarding loan transaction are pending between the petitioner and respondent.

Vide order dated 22.11.2017 Hon'ble CA No. 77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 19 OF 25 Justice Shri A.K. Pathak observed that "it is also noted that litigation regarding loan transactions are pending between the petitioner and respondent.

Petitioner has filed complaint cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 against the respondent before the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, which are pending in the said cases, it is alleged that petitioner had advanced loans to respondent on two occasions and to repay the loan, respondent had issued cheques, but the same returned dishonoured.
The documents placed on record show that two Loan Agreements were executed between the petitioner and respondent on 17 th May, 2013 and 20th November, 2013.
It is surprising that documents were executed in respect of the loan transactions but not in respect of business transactions regarding supply of goods.
The whole story projected regarding placing of orders for supply of goods and advance payment appears to be unrealistic."
However the said observations no where casts doubt on the execution of loan agreements and neither did it decide the validity of the loan agreement.

10.10 It is further contended that the Ld. MM failed to appreciate the Birendra Shukla vs Virendra Rana on 12 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/100947001/
10 evidence of Shri Hari Krishan Shreshta; that CW-1 has stated in his complaint that Rs.50 lacs was given in the presence of one Shri Hari Krishan Shreshtha who also witnessed the agreement and handing over of cash to the accused but

later on retracted from his statement that Rs.50 lacs was given in presence of Shri Hari Krishan Shreshtha and further changed his stand and deposed that it was wrongly mentioned that Hari Krishan Shreshtha also witnessed the CA No. 77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 20 OF 25 agreement; that the said Shri Hari Krishan Shrestha was produced in defence evidence as DW-2 and he has deposed that " on 17.05.2013 only Rs.25 lacs by way of cheque was given to Birender Shukla by Virender Rana; that Birender Rana returned Rs.6 lacs to Virender Rana on two occasions."

The point to be noted here is that the complainant has relied on agreement Ex.CW1/A which was no where witnessed by any Hari Krishan Shrestha rather the witnesses who witnessed the said agreement are Bobby Gill,
Rajeev Malhotra and Sangeeta.
He just tried to mix agreement dated 20.11.2013 with the agreement in question.

The said agreement was exhibited as Ex.CW1/D-1 (colly.)
during the cross examination of complainant.
However there is no connecting link between the agreement in question and the agreement dated 20.11.2013.

Rather in the agreement dated 20.11.2013 complainant paid Rs.34,40,000/- to the accused in cash which is going contrary to the plea of accused regarding challenge to the capacity of the complainant to lend money and that agreement was witnessed by Shri Hari Krishan Shrestha and Major Singh Gill.
The accused has tried to confuse two agreements which has no interlinked clause between themselves.

Assuming that the agreement Ex. CW1/A was witnessed by DW-2 Sh. Hari Krishan even then accused has failed to prove his stand that no cash amount was handed over to the accused as per terms of agreement Ex. CW1/A since he has admitted in his cross- examination that Virender Rana i.e. complainant paid Rs. 25 lacs in cash to Birender Shukla after two to three days of payment of Rs. 25 CA No. 77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS.
VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 21 OF 25 lacs by cheque and the said amount was given as loan.

Henceforth the Ld. Trial Court has rightly held that .. " Both the agreements i.e. agreement dated 17.05.2013 Ex.CW1/A and agreement dated 20.11.2013 which is part of Ex.CW1/D1 (colly), are separate agreements.
The Ld.
Counsel for accused has tried his level best to confuse CW1/complainant by putting the mixed questions with regard to both the agreements.

But complainant stood the test of cross- examination and explained that a separate amount of Rs.34.40 lacs was given to the accused for which agreement dated 20.11.2013 was executed."
10.11

It is further contended by the appellant that the Ld. M.M. failed to appreciate that even if the contents of agreement dated 07.05.2013 are considered to be proved then also the cheque was presented prematurely; that admittedly complainant has received certain amount in respect of the cheque in question and further the accused has paid a sum of Rs.18,00,000/- to him.

The agreement Ex.CW1/A contains the clause that "that second party is bound to pay Rs.6,00,000/- after every 45 days if they fail to pay the interest then whole will become due as interest on amount, which five cheques become due." CW-1
has deposed that "The loan was repayable with interest as specified in the above stated agreement dated 17.05.2013.

The accused was liable to pay as interest, a sum of Rs.
Birendra Shukla vs Virendra Rana on 12 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/100947001/
11 6 lacs every 45 days.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The accused only paid the first installment of interest of Rs. 6 lacs, that too belatedly.

Thereafter, the accused completely failed to pay the interest on the due dates as CA No.
77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 22 OF 25 contemplated under the agreement; that thus, in terms of the agreement, the entire debt and liability of Rs. 50 lakhs became due and I became immediately entitled to deposit all 5 cheques towards discharge of the debt and liability of Rs. 50 lakhs".

CA No.
77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The said fact got confirmed during his cross examination when a question was asked that as per clause (4) of Ex.CW1/A accused was bound to pay Rs.6 lacs after every 45 days and no suggestion was given from the side of the accused that accused was in fact was regularly paying the said interest amount.
This part of his testimony went unchallenged, unrebutted and unshattered as the same has not been assailed by way of cross examination.
It is well settled principle of law that if any part of testimony is not challenged in the cross examination that is deemed to be admitted.

Secondly, the accused examined DW-2 Shri Hari Kishan Shrestha in his defence who has stated that accused returned Rs.6 lacs to the complainant on two occasions but admittedly there is no receipt of the second payment of Rs.6 lacs nor there is any other record from which it can be said that accused in fact paid Rs.18 lacs to the complainant.
10.12 Henceforth the Ld. Trial Court has rightly held that " As per clause number 4 of loan agreement Ex.CWI1A, the accused was liable to pay Rs.6 lacs after every 45 days as interest.
It is also mentioned that in case accused failed to pay the interest the whole amount shall become due.
Complainant has admitted that only one installment of Rs.6 lacs was paid by the accused in terms of clause number 4 of the loan agreement Ex.CW1/A.

Whereas accused has CA No. 77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 23 OF 25 alleged that he had paid three installments of Rs.6 lacs each and out of these three installments, two installments were paid in the presence of Hari Kishan.
No documentary evidence has been placed on record to prove the payment of Rs.18 lacs.
The oral testimony of DW2 Hari Kishan cannot be relied upon because in other case bearing CC No.13/14/14, PS GK-I, he has deposed that on behalf of complainant and against accused.
His testimony is not creditworthiness.
Thus, accused has failed to prove that he repaid Rs.18 lacs towards the payment of principal amount.
The payment of Rs.6 lacs was admitted by the complainant made to pay interest and not to pay the principal amount."
11. Hence the accused has failed to rebut the presumption u/s. 139 of the N.I. Act which says that cheque duly drawn was towards a debt or liability.

It has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in K.N. Beena vs. Muniyappan and Another (2001) 8 SCC 458 that "in view of the provisions of Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act read with Section 118 thereof, the Court had to presume that the cheque had been issued for discharging a debt or liability.

entities.text: K.N. Beena vs. Muniyappan and Another (2001) 8 SCC 458
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The said presumption was rebuttable and could be rebutted by the accused by proving the contrary.
But mere denial or rebuttal by the accused was not enough.
The accused had to prove by cogent evidence that there was no debt or liability."
The accused has failed to prove that he has no debt or liability towards the complainant rather he has admitted taking of loan of Rs.25,00,000/- from him.

11.1 A meaningful reading of the provisions of the Negotiable CA No. 77/2019 BIRENDRA SHUKLA VS. VIRENDRA RANA PAGE NO. 24 OF 25 Instruments Act including, in particular, Sections 20, 87 and 139, makes it amply clear that a person who signs a cheque and makes it over to the payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption that the cheque had been issued for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability.

It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person Birendra Shukla vs Virendra Rana on 12 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/100947001/
12
other than the drawer
, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer.

If the cheque is otherwise valid,
the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted.
12. In view of the aforesaid discussion, I find no illegality or material irregularity in the impugned judgment dated 20.12.2018 and order on sentence dated 03.01.2019 passed by Ld. Trial Court.
There is no valid ground for interference with the conviction and sentence imposed on the appellant and the present appeal deserves to be dismissed and is accordingly dismissed.
The conviction of the appellant as passed by the Ld. MM is hereby upheld.
13. Copy of this order be sent to the Ld. Trial court alongwith trial court record.
File of the present appeal be consigned to record room.

Section 91, inter alia, stipulates that where the terms of contract or of a grant or any other disposition of property have been reduced to a form of written document - no evidence shall be given in proof of the terms of such a contract, grant or other disposition of property, except the document itself.
Therefore, if there is a written contract executed, neither party can claim that the terms of the contract or the nature of transaction/disposition is, in fact, different from that contained in the document itself.
The terms were specifically set out in the loan agreement and in view of the bar contained in section 91, it is not open to the accused to claim that the said document was never acted upon moreso when he admits the receipt of Rs. 25 lacs through the cheque as mentioned in the agreement.
The terms of agreement completely ruled out the so- called understanding between the parties.
